extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, crisis managers, organizational leaders, emergency managers, students and researchers studying crisis management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how organizations should prepare for, respond to, communicate about, and recover from disruptive unexpected events (crises). Covers crisis definitions, types, planning, leadership competencies, communication, continuity, and lessons from case studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements defining a crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Three elements are common to a crisis: (a) a threat to the organization, (b) the element of surprise, and (c) a short decision time. A fourth defining quality is the need for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If change is not needed, the event could more accurately be described as a failure or incident. Use these elements to distinguish crises from other disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of crisis management
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of crisis management is to be well prepared for crisis, ensure a rapid and adequate response to the crisis, maintain clear lines of reporting and communication in the event of crisis and agree rules for crisis termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisis management is situation-based and should include clear roles, responsibilities, and processes company-wide covering prevention, assessment, handling and termination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis response areas / phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The response shall include action in the following areas: crisis prevention, crisis assessment, crisis handling, and crisis termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include steps from understanding the influence of the crisis to preventing, alleviating, and overcoming different types of crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish metrics to define what constitutes a crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing metrics to define what scenarios constitute a crisis and should consequently trigger the necessary response mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define objective criteria and thresholds so organizations know when to invoke crisis plans rather than treating events inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a documented crisis-management plan (BS11200 referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis-management methods of a business or an organization are called a crisis-management plan. A British Standard BS11200:2014 provides a useful foundation for terminology and frameworks relating to crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans should account for corporate exposure to strategic 'black swan' events; work is ongoing to develop international standards—use recognized standards as foundations for plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis mindset and contingency planning
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'crises mindset' requires the ability to think of the worst-case scenario while simultaneously suggesting numerous solutions. Trial and error is accepted; maintain a list of contingency plans and always be on alert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations should be prepared with rapid response plans, perform analysis, drills and exercises, and keep contingency plans to fall back on if first-line responses fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and consistent internal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be open and consistent communication throughout the hierarchy to contribute to a successful crisis-communication process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear lines of reporting and internal information flows are critical so that decision makers and front-line staff act coherently during crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify crisis type to determine strategy (Lerbinger's eight types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different crises necessitate the use of different crisis management strategies. Lerbinger categorized eight types: Natural disaster; Technological crisis; Confrontation; Malevolence; Organizational Misdeeds; Workplace Violence; Rumours; Terrorist attacks / man-made disasters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the crisis early so that response strategies (e.g., technical fixes, public-facing apologies, security responses) match the nature and stakeholders of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal detection (early warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signal detection is the stage in a crisis in which leaders should sense early warning signals (red flags) that suggest the possibility of a crisis. Detection stages include sense-making and perspective-taking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop processes to notice, interpret, and escalate subtle indications of trouble; use sense-making and perspective-taking to avoid being blindsided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: During preparation and prevention organizations begin preparing for or averting crises foreshadowed in signal detection. Using an impact/probability model allows fairly accurate prediction of crisis scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak truth to power to predict worst-case scenarios; engage in planning, resource pre-positioning and training; learn from organizations experienced in emergency response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment and damage control
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of crisis containment and damage control is to limit reputational, financial, safety, and other threats to firm survival and bring the crisis to an end as quickly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act quickly to limit negative publicity and harm; prioritize immediate protective actions while preparing communication and recovery steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business recovery (continuity & resilience)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a crisis hits, organizations must carry on business while planning recovery. Crisis handlers engage in continuity planning and actively pursue organizational resilience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify critical functions and resources needed to keep operations running and plan how to restore normal operations amid ongoing crisis conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning from crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: In the wake of a crisis, decision makers adopt a learning orientation and use prior experience to develop new routines and behaviors that ultimately change the way the organization operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture lessons, update procedures and plans, and institutionalize improvements discovered during the incident and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis communication: three essential preparatory steps
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 3 essential steps an organization can take to prepare for and withstand a communications crisis: 1) Define your philosophy; 2) Assess your vulnerabilities; 3) Develop a protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a clear communication philosophy (e.g., transparency level), inventory vulnerabilities that could lead to reputational harm, and predefine protocols for internal/external messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated spokesperson(s) & media cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan should clearly stipulate that the only people to speak to publicly about the crisis are the designated persons, such as the company spokesperson or crisis team members. Ideally it should be one spokesperson who can be available on call at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperate with media, assure timely answers, explain what was done to resolve the situation; speed, accuracy and transparency in early hours are critical; avoid manipulated or incorrect information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingency planning details (speed, accuracy, long-term effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first hours after a crisis are most crucial; the plan should indicate how quickly each function should be performed. Information should be accurate and transparent. The contingency plan should help decision makers consider both short-term and long-term effects of every decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize actions, time-to-action standards, and include guidance on reputational as well as operational consequences of choices taken during crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business continuity planning criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When a crisis will cause significant disruption, a business continuity plan helps minimize disruption: identify critical functions/processes; conduct business impact analysis; create contingency plans for each critical function; test by rehearsal; periodically review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing and realistic simulations improve readiness; external exercise designers can improve realism; follow-up debriefings are essential to link simulation learnings to real-world changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information flow and command networks (structural-functional requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing information to an organization in a time of crisis is critical. Structural-functional systems theory identifies information flow in organizations as networks made up of members and command levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design clear information networks and command hierarchies so messages, decisions, and orders flow reliably under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of apologies, compensation and sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate about apologies: apology can open an organization up for possible legal consequences. Evidence indicates compensation and sympathy, two less expensive strategies, are as effective as an apology in shaping perceptions because they focus on victims' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance legal counsel with reputational strategy; consider compensation/sympathy responses where appropriate to address victims' needs without unnecessary legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis leadership competencies (James)
rubrics_metrics.description: James identifies five leadership competencies which facilitate organizational restructuring during and after a crisis: Building an environment of trust; Reforming the organization's mindset; Identifying obvious and obscure vulnerabilities; Making wise and rapid decisions as well as taking courageous action; Learning from crisis to effect change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leadership behavior directly affects public trust and the organization's capacity to restructure and recover—develop these competencies proactively through training and HR development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media strategy and monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media accelerates the speed that information spreads and empowers stakeholders; this can be mitigated by training, policy, and the right social media monitoring tools to detect signs of a crisis breaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include social media strategy in crisis plans, use monitoring to track stakeholder sentiment in real time, and be ready to respond quickly to online developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include media representative in Crisis Management Team (CMT)
rubrics_metrics.description: A media reaction plan should include a company media representative as part of the Crisis Management Team. All CMT members should understand how to deal with the media and be prepared to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and train CMT for media interactions; simulate interviews and press briefings as part of exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management strategy (CMS) fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis management strategy is a corporate development strategy designed to prevent crisis and support follow-up company advancement; it includes projection of the future based on ongoing monitoring of internal and external environments, selection and implementation of crisis prevention strategy and operating management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make CMS part of strategic management, combining monitoring, prediction and implementation of prevention/mitigation measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management model (arc and phases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilburg's crisis arc consists of crisis avoidance, crisis mitigation and crisis recovery. Another description: diagnosis of impending trouble, choosing appropriate turnaround strategy, implementation of change process and monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these phase models to structure planning: detect and diagnose early, select fitting turnaround strategies, clearly implement and monitor actions through recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyber crisis management planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional IT incident response plans often fail to consider cross-organizational activities needed for resilience in a major cyber crisis. A cyber crisis management plan reduces risks through careful pre-planning and requires a holistic, integrated and validated approach tailored to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build cross-functional cyber crisis plans that include business, legal, communications and technical teams; validate plans through integrated exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from case studies: best-practice communication actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (Tylenol, Odwalla, Mattel, Pepsi) show best practices: rapid recall or protective action; CEO visibility and direct communication; daily press briefings; express remorse, apology and accept responsibility; explain risks and actions for consumers; develop and communicate fixes; use media relations and advertising to inform and restore confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emulate timeliness, transparency, responsibility-taking, frequent media engagement, and clear corrective action in communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common anti-patterns to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples (Bhopal, Ford-Firestone, Exxon Valdez) highlight blunders to avoid: poor cross-cultural communication, blaming consumers, blaming partners, saying little about corrective actions, acting defensively, lacking a communication plan or trained team, symbolic but ineffective interventions, and remote/ill-equipped media centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and eliminate these behaviors in plans and training; ensure culturally appropriate messaging and avoid defensiveness or scapegoating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation exercise design and debriefing
rubrics_metrics.description: Crisis-management teams can rehearse plans by developing simulated scenarios. Simulations can lack realism; external exercise designers can improve realism. Following exercises, a thorough and systematic debriefing must be conducted to draw lessons from the simulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design realistic scenarios, use outside designers to challenge organizational assumptions, and conduct structured after-action reviews to capture improvements.
